video_title: How to Keep Your Bitcoin Safe Without a Seed Phrase
gist: Clay Garrett, head of BitKey at Block, walks Natalie Brunell through his team's forensic investigation of the Coldcard entropy hack (a random-number-generator misconfiguration that let attackers drain wallets, with BitKey's on-chain analysis roughly doubling the known ~$40M loss figure) and then details BitKey's alternative security model: a 2-of-3 multisig where the customer holds a hardware key and a phone key while Block holds a server key, with no user-managed seed phrase. He describes the encryption-based recovery and inheritance system (SPAKE2-brokered recovery contacts, a 7-day recovery delay, a 6-month inheritance claim window), BitKey's internal controls (two-reviewer merges, three separate production signing groups, multi-environment reproducible builds), and argues the hack is pushing users to reshape rather than abandon self-custody.

insights.claim: The Coldcard wallet compromise was caused by a firmware misconfiguration that routed key-generation entropy through a deterministic software random number generator instead of the intended hardware RNG, making seeds predictable and brute-forceable.
insights.speaker: Clay Garrett, head of BitKey at Block
insights.so_what: Entropy sourcing is now a first-order diligence question for any hardware wallet; investors and holders should treat 'which RNG, and is it actually wired up' as a checkable security property, not an assumption.
insights.quote: the code had a misconfiguration where it intended to route the entropy through the hardware random number generator

insights.claim: Because the Coldcard entropy source was deterministic, an attacker who knew the seed could predict every subsequent random number and simply iterate through the possibility space, checking the blockchain for funded addresses.
insights.speaker: Clay Garrett, head of BitKey at Block
insights.so_what: Deterministic-RNG bugs turn a wallet's entire user base into a cheaply searchable keyspace, meaning a single code defect can produce industry-scale losses rather than isolated incidents.
insights.quote: if you knew the seed, you could, you know, basically predict every random number that it would spit out

insights.claim: BitKey's investigation found that the vulnerability extended beyond the older Coldcard models and firmware versions named in Coldcard's own initial announcement, so later models were affected too.
insights.speaker: Clay Garrett, head of BitKey at Block
insights.so_what: Vendor advisories in a live incident can understate blast radius; holders should not treat a manufacturer's first scoping statement as final when funds are at stake.
insights.quote: initially it looked like only the you know kind of older models of gold card were affected after a certain firmware version

insights.claim: BitKey identified the attacker's transactions by a fingerprint of an unnecessarily high fixed fee rate of roughly 30 sats per vbyte, and used that pattern to find earlier blocks containing close to another $40 million in drained Bitcoin beyond the ~$40 million already known.
insights.speaker: Clay Garrett, head of BitKey at Block
insights.so_what: Loss totals from wallet exploits are discovered incrementally through on-chain pattern matching; early headline damage figures in such events are typically floors, not ceilings.
insights.quote: all of them used a very specific uh fee rate. So it was I think exactly 30 sats per vite which was quite high and unnecessary

insights.claim: One anomalous transaction led BitKey to hypothesize that a specific (unnamed) blockchain API services provider was used by the attacker; the provider checked its logs, confirmed BitKey's predicted evidence, and the material was handed to authorities.
insights.speaker: Clay Garrett, head of BitKey at Block
insights.so_what: Paid blockchain-infrastructure APIs are a deanonymization chokepoint — a reminder that the Bitcoin developer-services layer creates real KYC-linked forensic surface for attackers and, by extension, regulatory leverage.
insights.quote: a hypothesis that a specific blockchain services provider was used in the attack

insights.claim: BitKey is a 2-of-3 multisig in which the customer holds two keys (one on the hardware device, one generated on their mobile phone) and Block holds the third on its server, so Block cannot spend without the user and the user can spend without Block.
insights.speaker: Clay Garrett, head of BitKey at Block
insights.so_what: This is the key structural claim to verify when comparing collaborative-custody products: whether the service provider is a spending participant or only a recovery participant.
insights.quote: the customer owns two of the keys and bit key owns the third

insights.claim: All three BitKey keys are generated in three different environments (server, phone, hardware) with environment-specific entropy rather than a single shared key-generation library, so one library defect cannot compromise all three keys.
insights.speaker: Clay Garrett, head of BitKey at Block
insights.so_what: Multi-vendor / multi-environment key generation is the specific design property that would have contained a Coldcard-style RNG bug — a concrete differentiator to look for in wallet architecture.
insights.quote: all three keys are created in three different environments

insights.claim: BitKey verified after the Coldcard incident that all three of its keys were generated with 256 bits of entropy, and it runs periodic LLM-driven and manual security scans against its own codebase rather than only auditing after incidents.
insights.speaker: Clay Garrett, head of BitKey at Block
insights.so_what: Continuous automated code scanning is being positioned as table stakes for security-critical Bitcoin infrastructure — an ongoing operating cost, not a one-time audit line item.
insights.quote: all three keys that are part of bit key were generated with the desired amount of entropy they were all you know 256 bits of entropy

insights.claim: BitKey deliberately ships without a user-facing seed phrase, replacing it with a layered encryption scheme keyed to things the user already has — their cloud account, their unlocked hardware, and a trusted contact — so private keys are recoverable without the user becoming an operational-security expert.
insights.speaker: Clay Garrett, head of BitKey at Block
insights.so_what: If seed-phrase-free custody gains acceptance it materially widens the addressable market for self-custody hardware beyond technically confident users — the main growth constraint on the category.

insights.claim: BitKey encrypts the phone-held app key so it can be uploaded to the user's ordinary cloud storage, where it is useless to anyone who obtains it unless they also possess the user's unlocked hardware device to decrypt it.
insights.speaker: Clay Garrett, head of BitKey at Block
insights.so_what: Consumer cloud backup becomes a viable key-persistence layer when the decryption factor is a separate physical device — a pattern other wallet vendors are likely to copy.
insights.quote: we encrypt the app key allow you to upload it to your cloud. If someone gets access to that for any reason it's useless to them unless they have your unlocked hardware which can decrypt it

insights.claim: Garrett argues that seed-phrase difficulty is widely acknowledged privately but suppressed publicly by a Bitcoin cultural norm that treats self-managed seed phrases as the test of legitimacy, which distorts product feedback and slows adoption of alternatives.
insights.speaker: Clay Garrett, head of BitKey at Block
insights.so_what: Cultural gatekeeping, not technical merit, may be the main headwind for seed-phrase-free products — meaning distribution and narrative work matter as much as engineering for this category.
insights.quote: there is this sentiment that you know uh well if you don't you know have a seed phrase and keep it yourself you know you're not a real Bitcoiner

insights.claim: BitKey's recovery-contact setup shares its pairing code over the SPAKE2 password-authenticated key exchange protocol and deliberately routes the invite out of band, so Block cannot man-in-the-middle or observe what the user and their recovery contact exchange.
insights.speaker: Clay Garrett, head of BitKey at Block
insights.so_what: Provable exclusion of the service provider from the recovery channel is the technical answer to the 'you still have to trust Block' objection — a verifiable property worth auditing in any collaborative-custody offering.
insights.quote: the sort of code sharing mechanism is a security protocol called spake 2 and that makes sure that block is not able to sort of man in the middle

insights.claim: In BitKey's recovery flow the recovery contact only ever encrypts a special intermediary key, never a spending key, and the encrypted private key itself lives in the user's own cloud — so a user who loses both the hardware device and the phone can still recover.
insights.speaker: Clay Garrett, head of BitKey at Block
insights.so_what: Splitting 'who holds ciphertext' from 'who holds spending authority' is how social recovery avoids recreating a custodian; a useful template for evaluating competing recovery schemes.
insights.quote: We're not sending spending keys anywhere that's not you know like on your phone or in your cloud

insights.claim: A recovery initiated with only the unlocked hardware device triggers a 7-day waiting period during which BitKey's server notifies every communication channel on file daily and the legitimate owner can cancel from the app, so a thief holding a fingerprint-unlocked device still cannot take funds.
insights.speaker: Clay Garrett, head of BitKey at Block
insights.so_what: Time-delayed recovery with out-of-band alerting is the practical defense against physical device theft and duress; it should be a standard checklist item when comparing hardware wallets.
insights.quote: start a 7-day waiting period where the BitKey server will send notifications every day to all the communication channels we have on file

insights.claim: BitKey inheritance requires the beneficiary to hold their own BitKey account (possibly zero-balance) and uses a six-month uncancelled claim window before Block delivers an encrypted package it cannot itself decrypt to the beneficiary.
insights.speaker: Clay Garrett, head of BitKey at Block
insights.so_what: Built-in inheritance is a customer-acquisition flywheel — every enrolled beneficiary becomes a new account — and addresses the generational-transfer problem that keeps large holders on exchanges.
insights.quote: so it's a six-month waiting period

insights.claim: The updated BitKey hardware adds a screen that displays the destination address, amount and fee for hold-to-confirm approval on the device itself, a feature Block built in direct response to community feedback after the original screenless model.
insights.speaker: Clay Garrett, head of BitKey at Block
insights.so_what: On-device display closes the trusted-display gap that screenless signers cannot; its addition signals the product is converging on the security expectations of experienced self-custody users.

insights.claim: The screen's concrete threat model is the clipboard-replacement attack, where malware swaps a pasted destination address — a vector Garrett says is now virtually impossible on iOS but still possible on Android in certain configurations.
insights.speaker: Clay Garrett, head of BitKey at Block
insights.so_what: Address-substitution malware is a low-frequency but total-loss event; platform hardening has cut iOS exposure, leaving Android users as the residual risk population.
insights.quote: these were, you know, possible on on all platforms. Um, they've certainly been locked down now and um, virtually impossible on iOS. probably could still happen on Android in the right configurations

insights.claim: BitKey disables the common practice of merging on a stale approval, so every code change — including post-review fixes — requires a fresh second set of eyes before it can be merged.
insights.speaker: Clay Garrett, head of BitKey at Block
insights.so_what: The post-approval-change loophole is where security bugs slip into reviewed codebases; closing it is a cheap, checkable control that most software organizations leave open.
insights.quote: every code change that happens requires another set of eyes

insights.claim: BitKey uses three disjoint groups to sign production code for the app, the firmware and the server, with no person authorized on more than one path, and validates mobile releases by building in multiple environments plus a local developer laptop and comparing hashes.
insights.speaker: Clay Garrett, head of BitKey at Block
insights.so_what: This mirrors the 2-of-3 multisig ethos at the release-pipeline layer and is a defense against both insider threat and build-environment supply-chain compromise — a differentiator competitors would have to match.
insights.quote: we have three different groups that can sign production code. So we have code that gets pushed to the app to the firmware and to the server

insights.claim: Garrett says LLM-based security scanning of BitKey's open-source repo by outside community members has found issues the internal team missed, and predicts continuous 24/7 automated code scanning will become an industry standard for security-sensitive Bitcoin software.
insights.speaker: Clay Garrett, head of BitKey at Block
insights.so_what: Open-sourcing wallet code now yields a free AI-augmented audit workforce, shifting the cost-benefit of closed-source firmware (as Coldcard used) sharply toward disclosure.
insights.quote: if you're in this type of security sensitive space, you need to be running, you know, 24/7 scans against your code where possible

insights.claim: Garrett frames unequal access to frontier AI models as a security asymmetry: Block has access to frontier models many defenders lack, while less-restricted overseas models are available to attackers who face no comparable usage limits.
insights.speaker: Clay Garrett, head of BitKey at Block
insights.so_what: AI-model access tiering is becoming a competitive moat in security-critical crypto infrastructure — favoring large, well-capitalized issuers over independent hardware-wallet vendors.
insights.quote: there are areas of of the world where you know people who would do things that are are bad don't have that same limitation

insights.claim: Garrett reports that after the Coldcard incident nearly everyone he has spoken with is reshaping their self-custody setup — often single-sig users moving toward multisig — rather than abandoning self-custody for exchanges, and says he is more bullish on Bitcoin self-custody than before.
insights.speaker: Clay Garrett, head of BitKey at Block
insights.so_what: If the hack drives migration from single-sig to multisig rather than back to exchanges, it is a demand catalyst for collaborative-custody products rather than a sector-wide setback.
insights.quote: Almost everyone I've talked to is trying to figure out what the right shape of self- custody is for them compared to where they were

insights.claim: Garrett argues that a decline in self-custody would concentrate monetary influence in large exchanges — a centralization the Bitcoin network does not need — and cites account limits and login lockouts as the personal risk of exchange custody.
insights.speaker: Clay Garrett, head of BitKey at Block
insights.so_what: The self-custody-versus-exchange share of Bitcoin supply is a structural variable for the network's governance and censorship-resistance narrative, and therefore for its long-term monetary premium.
insights.quote: if self- custody goes away, like that's the centralization that the network does not need

insights.claim: Block recently launched auto-DCA between Cash App and BitKey, letting users set a Cash App balance threshold above which Bitcoin is automatically swept into self-custody, with discounted fees because of the in-house Cash App relationship.
insights.speaker: Clay Garrett, head of BitKey at Block
insights.so_what: Vertically integrating exchange-to-self-custody flow lowers both friction and fees versus third-party stacks — a distribution advantage standalone hardware-wallet makers cannot replicate.
insights.quote: we just recently launched uh auto DCA

insights.claim: BitKey is openly considering architecture changes in response to post-hack feedback, including a configuration with two hardware devices plus the BitKey server key and the possibility of letting users import their own seeds, with no commitments made yet.
insights.speaker: Clay Garrett, head of BitKey at Block
insights.so_what: Seed import would remove the biggest objection sovereign-minded Bitcoiners raise against BitKey; watch for it as the signal that Block is going after the hardcore self-custody segment, not just newcomers.
insights.quote: what would it mean, for example, to let people import their seeds? Um, we've made no commitments on that yet
